# How a CPU Cache Hierarchy Works: A Technical Explanation

## The Memory Wall Problem

Modern processors execute instructions at multi-gigahertz clock rates, yet DRAM access latency has stubbornly remained in the range of 50–100 nanoseconds—equivalent to hundreds of CPU cycles. This growing gap between processor speed and main memory latency is known as the "memory wall." The cache hierarchy exists to bridge this gap by exploiting two fundamental properties of real programs: **temporal locality** (recently accessed data is likely to be accessed again soon) and **spatial locality** (data near recently accessed addresses is likely to be accessed soon). By staging data in progressively larger, slower memories, the hierarchy presents the illusion of a large, fast memory at a fraction of the cost of building one from SRAM.

## The Hierarchy Levels

A typical modern design uses three levels of cache between the CPU cores and DRAM, each characterized by a trade-off among capacity, latency, associativity, and sharing.

**L1 cache** is the smallest and fastest, typically 32–64 KB per core, with access latencies of roughly 4–5 cycles. It is usually split into separate instruction (L1i) and data (L1d) caches so that instruction fetch and data loads can proceed in parallel without structural hazards. L1 is virtually indexed and physically tagged in many designs to allow address translation to overlap with cache lookup.

**L2 cache** is larger—typically 256 KB to 2 MB per core—with latencies around 10–15 cycles. It is usually unified (holding both instructions and data) and private to each core. L2 serves as the backing store for L1 misses and is often designed with higher associativity than L1 to reduce conflict misses.

**L3 cache** (last-level cache, LLC) is shared among all cores on a die, ranging from a few megabytes to over 100 MB in server parts, with latencies of 30–50 cycles. The LLC absorbs traffic from all cores and filters requests to DRAM. Modern designs often use non-uniform cache architectures (NUCA), where the LLC is banked into slices connected by an on-chip interconnect, and each core has a faster path to nearby slices.

## Organization: Sets, Ways, and Lines

Every cache is organized as an array of **cache lines** (also called blocks), typically 64 bytes on x86 and ARM. A memory address is decomposed into three fields: the **offset** (bits selecting a byte within the line), the **index** (bits selecting a set), and the **tag** (the remaining high-order bits). The cache is divided into S sets, each holding W ways; the total capacity is S × W × line size. This is a **set-associative** organization: a given address maps to exactly one set but can occupy any of the W ways within it.

Associativity is a crucial design parameter. A direct-mapped cache (W = 1) is simple and fast but suffers conflict misses when two hot addresses map to the same set. Fully associative caches (one set, many ways) eliminate conflict misses but require expensive parallel tag comparison. Real designs choose intermediate associativity—8- or 16-way is common at L2/L3—to balance hit rate against access latency and area.

On a lookup, the index selects a set, and all W tags in that set are compared simultaneously against the address tag. A match with the valid bit set constitutes a hit; otherwise, a miss triggers a refill from the next level.

## Replacement, Write Policy, and Coherence

On a miss, the cache must choose a victim line to evict. **LRU** (least recently used) is the classic policy, but exact LRU is expensive for high associativity, so real caches approximate it—for example, with tree-based pseudo-LRU or, in many Intel and AMD designs, adaptive policies informed by reuse-distance prediction. Victim caches and stream buffers can further reduce the cost of evictions and prefetching.

**Write policy** determines how stores interact with the hierarchy. A write-back cache defers writing to the next level until the line is evicted, marking it dirty with a per-line dirty bit; this reduces memory traffic at the cost of coherence complexity. A write-through cache updates the next level immediately. Most L1/L2 caches are write-back with write-allocate: on a store miss, the line is fetched before being modified. L3 and beyond increasingly use non-inclusive or exclusive policies—e.g., AMD's "victim cache" L3 and Intel's non-inclusive LLCs—to avoid duplicating data across levels.
